items.prompt: Per L1, what is "documentation discipline"?
choices: The consistent habit of confirming verbal decisions in writing, close to when they happen, regardless of whether a dispute seems likely at the time
A formal legal process for recording every workplace conversation
A habit reserved only for conversations a person expects to be disputed later
Keeping detailed personal notes that are never shared with anyone else
items.explanation: L1 defines documentation discipline as a consistent habit applied regardless of anticipated disputes, not a reactive tool used only when trouble seems likely.
items.reference:
Reactive

Only write it down once trouble seems likely

Discipline

Confirm verbal decisions as a routine habit, every time

Why: a habit applied only when trouble seems likely is itself what reads as paranoid — the discipline is in doing it consistently, before anyone suspects a dispute.
items.learnMore:
A habit, not a reflex

Documentation discipline is defined by when it's applied, not by whether writing happens at all.

Reactive note-takingDocumentation discipline
TriggerA dispute seems likelyAny verbal decision with real stakes
How it readsDefensive, suspiciousRoutine, professional
Who it protectsOnly the person worried about a disputeEveryone in the conversation, including the decision-maker

The engineer in the Scenario had no habit of confirming verbal decisions at all — not just no record of this one.

Common mistake

Deciding in the moment whether "this one" seems risky enough to write down. By the time it looks risky, you're already in reactive territory, which is exactly what reads as paranoid.

items.prompt: What is a "written confirmation", per L1?
choices: A short, neutral message sent after a verbal decision, restating what was agreed so there's a shared, dated record
A formal contract requiring both parties' signatures
A performance review written at the end of the year
A message sent only after a dispute has already started
items.explanation: L1 defines a written confirmation as a short, neutral, promptly-sent message that restates the agreed decision.
items.reference:
📝 Restates the specific decision
🧭 Names the reasoning given, if any
📅 Dated, just by existing

Why: a written confirmation only works as evidence later if it actually restates what was decided, not just that a conversation took place.
items.learnMore:
What a confirmation actually has to do

A written confirmation isn't a thank-you note — it's a short, neutral record of a specific decision.

PartExample
The decision"We're shipping without the security review this sprint"
The reasoning"given the schedule pressure"
The dateImplicit — the message's own timestamp

Sent right after the conversation, this is short enough to take thirty seconds and specific enough to resolve a dispute three weeks later.

Common mistake

Writing "thanks for the chat earlier" and treating it as equivalent. It proves a conversation happened, not what was decided in it.

items.learnMore:

items.prompt: Per L1, what fear typically stops people from documenting verbal decisions?
choices: That sending a confirmation will feel like publicly doubting a colleague's word
That documentation is against company policy in most organizations
That written confirmations take too long to write
That colleagues will not read the confirmation at all
items.explanation: L1 names the fear of looking distrustful or paranoid as the main thing that stops people from documenting decisions.
items.reference:
😬 Fear: "this looks like I doubt them"
🚫 Result: the decision never gets written down anywhere

Why: this fear is about how documenting feels in the moment, not about whether it actually reads as paranoid once sent well.
items.learnMore:
The fear vs. the actual outcome

The fear that stops people is almost entirely anticipatory — imagining how sending a confirmation will feel, rather than how it will actually read.

"Sending this feels like publicly doubting them"
↓
Confirmation goes unsent
↓
No record exists if memory later diverges

L2 resolves this fear directly: a well-framed confirmation doesn't actually read as distrustful at all — see the paranoid-vs-professional table.

Common mistake

Treating the discomfort of sending the message as evidence it will land badly. The discomfort is about the writer's own anticipation, not about how a neutral, well-timed confirmation actually reads.

items.prompt: What is a "paper trail," per L1, as distinct from a single written confirmation?
choices: The accumulated set of written confirmations, emails, and notes that, taken together, establish what was actually decided and when
A single email sent once, regardless of whether more decisions follow
A formal legal filing kept by HR
A verbal summary given at the end of a project
items.explanation: L1 defines a paper trail as the accumulated set of records over time — one confirmation starts it, but the trail itself is the ongoing habit.
items.reference:
✉️ One written confirmation
➕ Another written confirmation
📚 = a paper trail, over time

Why: a paper trail isn't one email — it's what a habit of writing confirmations adds up to, which is why the habit matters more than any single message.
items.learnMore:
One message vs. a trail

A single confirmation resolves a single dispute. A paper trail is what accumulates when the habit is consistent.

TermScope
Written confirmationOne decision, one message
Paper trailThe accumulated set, over time, establishing a pattern

The engineer in the Scenario had neither — not one confirmation and certainly no accumulated trail — which is why the dispute came down to memory alone.

Common mistake

Thinking one confirmation email, sent once, is the same as "having a paper trail." It's a start, not the habit itself.
